teaching.task: # Year 12 Physics M8 V05: Fusion in main-sequence stars. Why do main-sequence stars release energy by combining light nuclei? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: First, how a star switches on. A cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen, collapses under its own gravity. As it falls inwards, gravitational potential energy becomes thermal energy, and the core heats up. At about ten million kelvin, the core starts fusing hydrogen, and the star ignites. Now the hot core pushes outwards with pressure, balancing gravity pulling inwards. That balance makes a main-sequence star. And it corrects itself. If fusion runs too fast, the core expands and cools, and fusion slows down. Fusing protons is hard. They're both positive, so they repel each other. Only at millions of kelvin do they move fast enough to get close, and even then, most bounce off. The force that holds a nucleus together only reaches about the width of a proton, so protons must almost touch. That's why fusion needs such a hot, dense core, and why the Sun burns slowly enough to last about ten billion years. So why does energy come out? Protons and neutrons, called nucleons, attract each other through the strong nuclear force. When they come together, they drop into a lower energy state, like a ball dropping into a hole, and that energy leaves. So a nucleus has less mass than its separate parts. The energy you'd need to pull it apart again is its binding energy. For helium four, that's twenty-eight point three MeV, about seven MeV for every nucleon.

**Boundary:** starts on v04's final frame (the HR diagram with the main sequence glowing and the Sun's core inset "4 ¹H → ⁴He ?"). Teaches: a star's ignition (gas cloud collapse, gravitational potential energy to thermal energy, about 10⁷ K) and hydrostatic equilibrium as the main-sequence state, with its self-correction; why fusion is hard (Coulomb repulsion; the strong force's short range; hot, dense cores; slow burning); binding energy and the mass defect from E = mc²; the binding-energy-per-nucleon curve (rises steeply, peaks near iron, falls slowly) and why combining light nuclei releases energy; the proton-proton chain, step by step, with conservation of nucleon number and charge; the net reaction; the energy from atomic masses (0.028697 u, 26.7 MeV, 0.7%); the CNO cycle as a catalyst cycle with the same net result; why it needs a hotter core (charge 6: at the same separation, six times the repulsion) and dominates in stars above about 1.3 solar masses; the Sun's 1% CNO share, confirmed by solar CNO neutrinos (2020). Stops before helium burning, later stages, the iron limit as an end point and neutron capture (v06), fission (later Module 8 lessons), lepton number (named only), quantum tunnelling (author note b).

## Decisions

- **Learner question (route wording kept).** "Why do main-sequence stars release energy by combining light nuclei?" The answer: nucleons attract through the strong force, so a nucleus has less mass than its parts (binding energy, 4); light nuclei are loosely bound per nucleon, so joining them climbs the binding-energy curve and the lost mass leaves as energy, E = Δmc² (5, 8); a hot, dense core makes the joining possible against repulsion, and gravity keeps the core there (2, 3); stars do it by two routes, the pp chain and the CNO cycle (6 to 11).
- **Hook (v04's handoff; m7-v16 recalled).** 3 s prediction chips: "more mass", "less mass", "the same". Answer: less, by about 0.7%.
- **Ignition and balance (site lesson 6 `ignite-a-star-and-balance-it`).** Collapse converts gravitational potential energy to thermal energy (Year 11 energy); fusion begins near 10⁷ K (site "~10 million K"); hydrostatic equilibrium (outward pressure of hot gas and radiation against gravity; site "Analyse 7 marks" step 1 wording: "Gravity versus fusion is loose: fusion supplies the energy, pressure resists the collapse") as the definition of a main-sequence star; the self-correcting "thermostat".
- **Why fusion is hard (new causal step).** Like charges repel (Year 11); the strong force reaches only about a proton's width, so protons must almost touch; most collisions fail; so fusion needs a hot, dense core and proceeds slowly. Quantum tunnelling is in author note b only.
- **Binding energy (site lesson 7 `read-the-binding-energy-curve`, vocabulary "Mass defect").** Defined from E = mc² (m7-v16): a nucleus has less mass than its separate nucleons; the binding energy is the energy needed to separate them. Helium-4: 28.3 MeV, 7.1 MeV per nucleon. The "ball dropping into a hole" analogy is used once (author note c).
- **Binding-energy curve (site Figure 1; kit limit).** Coded curve, peak "near iron" (Fe-56 8.79 MeV labelled; Ni-62 noted in author note d, as the site's own HSC tip says); hydrogen-1 at zero; "climbing the curve releases energy". The curve's falling side (fission) is drawn but not narrated beyond one tag (fission is later in Module 8).
- **pp chain (syllabus example; site lesson 6 net equation).** Three steps shown as nuclear equations with mass and atomic numbers: ¹H + ¹H → ²H + e⁺ + ν (slow, a proton becomes a neutron); ²H + ¹H → ³He + γ; ³He + ³He → ⁴He + 2 ¹H; steps 1 and 2 twice. Net: 4 ¹H → ⁴He + 2e⁺ + 2ν. The positrons annihilate with electrons (m7-v16 recalled). This is the main (pp I) branch; other branches in author note e.
- **Conservation (route "conservation").** Nucleon number and charge checked on step 1 in narration and on every step on screen; "the neutrino keeps a third quantity balanced, which you'll meet later in this module" (lepton number; Module 8 particle lessons).
- **Energy (route "mass-energy release"; site Stop and Check uses nuclear masses).** Atomic masses: 4 × 1.007825 − 4.002603 = 0.028697 u; × 931.5 = 26.7 MeV (site 26.7 MeV); 0.71% of the mass. Why atomic masses: they include the electrons, so the positron annihilation energy is included (one sentence; author note f compares with the site's 25.7 MeV from nuclear masses, site note 16). The Sun's rate (8.9 × 10³⁷ reactions s⁻¹) is a screen tag only.
- **CNO cycle (syllabus example; site "Compare 6 marks").** Six steps on a coded ring: ¹²C + ¹H → ¹³N + γ; ¹³N → ¹³C + e⁺ + ν; ¹³C + ¹H → ¹⁴N + γ; ¹⁴N + ¹H → ¹⁵O + γ; ¹⁵O → ¹⁵N + e⁺ + ν; ¹⁵N + ¹H → ¹²C + ⁴He. Net the same as the pp chain; carbon is a catalyst (site "regenerated rather than consumed"). The narration walks the ring in one sentence; the screen shows each equation.
- **Why hotter (site "Compare 6 marks" step 3; Revision 2).** At the same separation, the proton-carbon repulsion is about 6 times the proton-proton repulsion (charge 6); the narration says "at the same distance" and both drawings share one marked separation; the CNO cycle dominates above about 1.3 solar masses (site "p-p chain dominant in stars < 1.3 M☉"), core above about 17 million K (author note g). The Sun's core about 15 million K; CNO about 1% of the Sun's energy, confirmed in 2020 by an underground neutrino detector in Italy (Borexino; named on screen; author note g).
- **Memory aid (scene 12, new): "Four protons in, one helium out, 0.7% lighter. The CNO cycle just borrows carbon."** See "Memory aid check".
- **Attempts (original, HSC style).** A1 (3 marks): the energy released in ³He + ³He → ⁴He + 2 ¹H with atomic masses given: 0.013805 u, 12.9 MeV. Crossed: forgetting the two product protons (Δm = 2 × 3.016029 − 4.002603 = 2.029 u, "1890 MeV"). A2 (3 marks, compare): pp chain against CNO cycle. Crossed: "the CNO cycle uses up carbon".
- **Significant figures.** Masses to six decimal places in u (as given); energies to three figures.

- **Site notes (quoted from the site, read 6 Nov; for root to log in `../site-corrections-phys-y12.md` if accepted; continuing after v04's note 15):**
  16. Mass defect without positrons (lesson 7 Stop and Check, Activity 1 and Q1): "Calculate the energy released when 4 protons fuse to form helium-4. (m_p = 1.007276 u, m_α = 4.001506 u)" with answer "Δm = 0.02760 u, E ≈ 25.7 MeV". With nuclear masses the reaction must include the two positrons (charge conservation: 4 p → α + 2e⁺ + 2ν), so the directly released energy is 25.7 − 1.02 = 24.7 MeV, and 26.7 MeV once the positrons annihilate. Lesson 6 states 26.7 MeV for the same reaction. Suggest using atomic masses (¹H 1.007825 u, ⁴He 4.002603 u, giving 26.7 MeV) or writing the full equation with positrons.

  18. History (lesson 6 retrieve and reflect): "Hans Bethe's 1939 calculation ... showed that the Sun fuses 600 million tonnes of hydrogen to helium every second via the pp chain". Bethe's 1939 paper described both the pp chain and the CNO cycle and concluded the CNO cycle powers the Sun (later revised); the 600 million tonnes figure follows from the Sun's luminosity, not from his paper. Suggest "showed how fusion could power stars".
  19. Extend task (lesson 7 retrieve and reflect): "in 5 billion years the Sun will have converted roughly 0.07% of its total mass into energy". At 3.83 × 10²⁶ W for 5 × 10⁹ years the mass converted is 6.7 × 10²⁶ kg, 0.034% of 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg. Suggest "about 0.03%" or "over 10 billion years, about 0.07%".

- **Cause chain taught, in order:** (1) gravity compresses and heats a gas cloud until its core can fuse; pressure then balances gravity, a stable main-sequence star (2); (2) protons repel, and the strong force acts only at touching range, so fusion needs a hot, dense core and is slow (3); (3) nucleons attract, so a nucleus has less mass than its parts: binding energy (4); (4) light nuclei are loosely bound per nucleon, so combining them climbs the curve and releases the mass difference as energy (5); (5) the pp chain does this in steps, conserving nucleon number and charge, and releases 26.7 MeV per helium (6 to 8); (6) the CNO cycle reaches the same result with carbon as a catalyst but needs higher temperatures, so stars above about 1.3 solar masses use it (9, 10).

- **Author notes (not learner copy):**

  (b) At 1.5 × 10⁷ K the mean proton kinetic energy (about 2 keV) is far below the Coulomb barrier (about 0.5 to 1 MeV); fusion happens through quantum tunnelling for the fastest protons. The pp chain's first step is also slow because it needs a weak interaction (a proton becoming a neutron), with a mean proton waiting time of billions of years. The narration says "most bounce off" and "this step is very slow", both true; tunnelling is not named (not in the syllabus).
  (c) The "ball dropping into a hole" analogy: its limit is that the hole's depth is the binding energy and the energy leaves as photons and kinetic energy of products; the narration says only that the energy leaves.

With nuclear masses, 4m_p − m_α = 0.027598 u = 25.71 MeV, which omits the positrons' 1.02 MeV of rest energy (site note 16).

The Revision 2 visual upgrade is already written into each scene's Visual line (anchor, simulation, colour roles, hand tags, framed answers). This section tops the design up to the checklist used for Year 11 Physics, Biology and Chemistry, and applies root rules R1 to R4 (`../checks/root-acceptance-y11-upgrade-12-nov.md`). Where a scene has an "Upgrade (Revision 3)" paragraph, it adds to the Visual and wins wherever the two differ. No narration line changed.

- **Board stages.** (A) last time's frame: the core inset on the painted Sun, scene 1 (about 29 s); (B) the painted gas cloud collapsing, scene 2 (about 38 s); (C) the colliding protons, scene 3 (about 30 s); (D) the mass-defect bars, scene 4 (about 34 s); (E) the binding-energy curve with its live marker, scene 5 (about 37 s); (F) the reaction steps, then the A and Z tallies under them, scenes 6 and 7 (about 70 s; the tallies arrive at about 35 s); (G) the working layout, scene 8 (about 36 s); (H) the CNO ring, scene 9 (about 41 s); (I) the Coulomb comparison, scene 10 (about 41 s); (J) the memory card, scene 11 (about 10 s); question and feedback cards; the handoff; the notes board. No set-up runs past about 70 s, so no cut was needed.
- **Simulation engines (`src/explainer/sims/`).** The colliding protons in scene 3 run on the particle box engine (`particle-box.ts`, drawn with `ParticleBoxView`): one species with a two-particle reaction that has an activation energy standing for the electrical repulsion. Drawn with `failed`, most collisions flash as bounces; raising the `temperature` timeline lets a few succeed, so "hotter core, more fusion" is counted (`rateAt`) and not just stated. The first pair that approaches and turns back is a `custom` run on the field motion engine with a repulsive 1/r² force. The binding-energy marker (scene 5) reads the design's table of values and stays lesson-coded.

Text a student must read is never faint: an earlier row that "dims" stays solid at a smaller size, and an earlier path that "stays faint" is a thin solid line in its role colour.
- **No coded drawings of real objects.** Apparatus and real objects are painted plates (the `y12p-` set or existing plates), scaled uniformly and never stretched. Exam-style outlines (ground, walls, cliffs, bench edges), vectors, field lines, graphs and circuit symbols stay coded, as root decision 3 for this course records.
- **No video numbers on screen.** Where a Visual line tags something with a video code, the on-screen words say "last time", "an earlier video" or "next time". Video codes in this document are notes for the builder.
- **Question cards.** Each attempt card arrives whole (sentences 38 px) with a picture from its first frame. The picture is answer-free: nothing on it can be counted, measured or read off to get the answer. Method aids (ledgers, formula strips, memory cards) are hidden while a countdown runs; every supplied value and condition stays on the card. scenes.teachingReason: First, how a star switches on. A cloud of gas, mostly hydrogen, collapses under its own gravity. scenes.teachingReason: Fusing protons is hard. They're both positive, so they repel each other. Only at millions of kelvin do they move fast enough to get close, and even then, most bounce off. That's why fusion needs such a hot, dense core, and why the Sun burns slowly enough to last about ten billion years.

scenes.teachingReason: So why does energy come out? Protons and neutrons, called nucleons, attract each other through the strong nuclear force. When they come together, they drop into a lower energy state, like a ball dropping into a hole, and that energy leaves. So a nucleus has less mass than its separate parts. The energy you'd need to pull it apart again is its binding energy. For helium four, that's twenty-eight point three MeV, about seven MeV for every nucleon.

scenes.teachingReason: Now plot binding energy per nucleon against mass number. It climbs steeply for light nuclei, peaks near iron, then slowly falls. Climbing the curve means the nucleons end up more tightly bound, so the products have less mass, and energy is released. Hydrogen one is a single proton, with no binding energy at all, and helium four is up at seven MeV per nucleon. So joining hydrogen into helium is a big climb, and a big release of energy. That's why combining light nuclei gives out energy.

scenes.teachingReason: In the Sun, the main route is the proton-proton chain. Step one, two protons fuse into deuterium. One proton turns into a neutron, giving out a positron and a neutrino. This step is very slow, and it's the main reason the Sun lasts so long. Step two, deuterium fuses with another proton to make helium three, giving out a gamma ray photon. Steps one and two happen twice. Step three, two helium three nuclei fuse into helium four, and two protons are set free.

scenes.teachingReason: Now the energy. Use atomic masses, which include the electrons, so the annihilation energy is counted too. Four hydrogen atoms have a mass of four point zero three one three u. One u is worth nine hundred and thirty-one point five MeV, so the energy released is about twenty-six point seven MeV. That's zero point seven per cent of the mass, the same figure we used for the Sun.

scenes.teachingReason: Stars more than about one point three times the Sun's mass mostly use a second route, the CNO cycle. A carbon twelve nucleus captures a proton, then another, then another, and another, turning into nitrogen and oxygen along the way, with two steps giving out a positron and a neutrino. At the last step, the nucleus splits into helium four and carbon twelve, the same carbon it started with. Carbon is a catalyst. It helps, but it isn't used up. The net result is the same, four protons into one helium four, and the same twenty-six point seven MeV.

scenes.teachingReason: Why do massive stars use it? Carbon has six protons, so at the same distance, a proton approaching it is repelled about six times as strongly. That needs a hotter core, above about seventeen million kelvin. The Sun's core is about fifteen million kelvin, so the proton-proton chain supplies about ninety-nine per cent of its energy. In twenty twenty, a detector deep under a mountain in Italy caught neutrinos from the Sun's CNO cycle, confirming the last one per cent. Massive stars have hotter cores, so for them, the CNO cycle dominates.
